unit.title: Money and inflation
unit.description: Why idle money loses value and how much your investment needs to earn to protect you

texts: Two salaries, two endings
Marta
Pablo
Marta earns €1,800 a month. Pablo, €1,300.
This month I bought some new trainers, ate out three times… and I've still got €50 left over!
I cook at home nearly all the time. I've got €300 left over and I put it aside.
In 5 years' time, without investing anything, who'll have more saved?
Marta, because she earns more
Marta puts aside €50 a month: **€3,000** in 5 years. Pablo puts aside €300: **€18,000**, six times as much.
Pablo, because he puts more aside each month
Exactly! Pablo builds up **€18,000** in 5 years and Marta €3,000. What counts is what you keep, not what you earn.
Both the same
No: Marta puts aside €50 a month and Pablo €300. In 5 years that's €3,000 versus €18,000.
And if Pablo invests that €300, compound interest makes the gap even bigger.
Earning a lot isn't the same as **having** a lot. Look at what Pablo has.
How much does he really have?
Pablo already invests part of what he puts aside. This is what he owns and what he owes: does it **add** or **subtract**?
Pablo's net worth
What he owns
What he owes
His emergency fund in the bank
It's his and he can use it any time: it adds.
His index ETF (what it's worth today)
What you've invested counts at what it's worth today: if the ETF goes up, his net worth goes up.
His car (what it's worth today)
It adds at what it's worth today, not what it cost, and it's worth less every year.
What's left on the car loan
A debt subtracts: the car isn't fully his yet.
His unpaid card balance
What you owe on your card subtracts, even if you can't see it.
Place everything and find out Pablo's net worth.
**Net worth = what you own − what you owe.** It's your real scoreboard: what you invest can grow over the years, the car loses value and debts subtract.
Watch out for debts: even if you can't see them, they subtract.
You're doing well! Watch how the sum below changes.
Tap **add** or **subtract** for each item

steps.title: Your real scoreboard
steps.body:
Your **salary** tells you how much comes in each month; your **net worth**, how much you have. There are two levers to grow it:

• **Put aside the difference** between what comes in and what goes out.
• **Invest it**, so it works for you.

What holds it back: spending every pay rise, expensive debt and idle money, which is worth a little less every year because of inflation.
steps.key: Wealth is net worth, not salary: what you own minus what you owe.
steps.tip: Try it: open Portfolio and see what all your virtual money is worth today.

texts: Grandma's 100 pesetas
Grandma Carmen
When I was your age, I'd come back from the market with a full basket for 100 pesetas.
Today 100 pesetas would be 60 cents. That wouldn't even get you a loaf of bread!
Why do you think that is?
Because things used to be lower quality
Quality has changed a bit, but that doesn't explain why **everything** goes up: bread is still bread.
Because prices go up a little every year and it builds up
That's it! It's called **inflation**. 3 % a year sounds like nothing… until 20 years go by.
Because the euro is worth less than the peseta
The exchange rate was 166.386 pesetas to the euro: that's not the problem. What matters is how much prices have risen since then.
Well, let's see if you understand it better than I do
Let's look at it with your own shopping basket.
Your basket in a few years
Today, **€50** gets you this whole basket. But prices go up every year with inflation…
Bread
Milk
Fruit
Pasta
Eggs
Chicken
Fish
Olive oil
Coffee
With 3 % inflation a year, what will those same €50 get you in 20 years' time?
Almost everything: 3 % is very little
About half the basket
Nothing: everything will cost ten times as much
3 % for 20 years pushes prices up by 81 %: your €50 buys what €28 buys today. Check it by moving the years.
Find the inflation rate that halves your basket in just 10 years.
**Idle money shrinks**: at 3 %, in 20 years it buys just over half. That's why money you won't need for years has to earn more than inflation.
Oof! That doesn't even fill a third of the basket. That's what high inflation feels like.
See? The notes are the same €50, but they buy much less.
Now turn the inflation up: what happens at 7 %?
Drag the years and see what happens to your basket

steps.title: Why prices go up
steps.body:
They rise when there's more money or more demand than things to buy, or when producing costs more (energy in 2022). In Spain it's measured by the INE (the national statistics office) with the **CPI**: in 2025 it averaged 2.7 %.

The ECB tries to keep it around **2 %** by raising or cutting interest rates.
steps.key: With inflation, money that sits still buys a little less every year.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, check whether the S&P 500 has risen more than inflation.

u1l3.title: The CPI and your shopping basket

texts: Why do I notice it more?
Leo
Sara
They say inflation is 3 %, but I feel like everything's going up way more than that.
Well, I barely notice it…
Leo rents a flat and drives everywhere. Sara lives with her family and gets around by bike.
This year, rent and petrol have gone up more than everything else. Who's right?
Leo's exaggerating: inflation is the same for everyone
The CPI is an **average**. Everyone has their own basket: if you spend more on what's rising most, your inflation is higher.
Both: each of them has their own inflation
That's it! The CPI is everyone's average. Leo spends a lot on rent and petrol, so **his** inflation is higher than 3 %.
Sara: if she doesn't notice it, there's no inflation
Just because Sara doesn't notice it doesn't mean prices aren't rising: her basket has less of what has gone up most.
The inflation that doesn't move as much
The INE gives two figures. **Headline CPI** measures the whole basket. **Core inflation** strips out what goes up and down very fast (energy and fresh food) to show the underlying trend.
Counts in core
Left out: very volatile
The electricity bill
It's energy: it can shoot up one month and drop the next.
A T-shirt
Clothes change price bit by bit: they count in core.
Fresh strawberries
Unprocessed food depends on the weather and the harvest: it's left out.
A haircut
Services change slowly: they're the underlying trend.
Filling up the tank
Fuel is energy: very volatile.
A packet of pasta
It's processed food: it stays in core.
Sort all six items.
If electricity shoots up one month, headline CPI jumps, but **core** barely moves. That's why central banks watch it so closely: it shows the underlying trend.
Hint: anything that depends on the weather or on oil is out.
In or out? Sort each item

steps.title: How it's measured and why the stock market watches it
steps.body:
Every month, Spain's statistics office (INE) records the prices of a **basket** of hundreds of goods and services. The **CPI** is how much that basket has changed compared with the same month the year before; each item is weighted by what households spend on it on average.

Investors wait for it closely: if it comes in higher than expected, the central bank is expected to raise interest rates, and that tends to move the stock market that same day.
steps.key: The CPI is everyone's average: your inflation depends on what you spend on.
steps.tip: Try it: on CPI day, watch how the S&P 500 moves in Market.

texts: Safe… or protected?
You have **€10,000** in an account that pays 0 %. The balance never goes down. But prices go up…
With 2.7 % inflation a year, what will those €10,000 buy in 10 years' time?
The same: the balance hasn't gone down
What about €7,700 buys today
What about €2,700 buys today
Over 10 years at 2.7 %, prices rise by 31 %: your €10,000 buys what €7,661 buys today. You don't lose euros, you lose **purchasing power**.
How much would the account need to pay so you don't lose purchasing power?
**Real return ≈ return − inflation.** You only gain purchasing power if your money earns more than prices go up.
Yikes! Your money shrinks really fast like this.
Still in the red: your euros are growing more slowly than prices.
Raise what the account pays until the line stops falling
«They're safe there»
Uncle Javi
I've had €20,000 in my account for years. At 0 %, but I'm not losing anything there.
What do you say to him?
You're right, the balance doesn't go down
The balance doesn't go down, but with 2.5 % inflation, in 15 years that €20,000 will buy what about **€13,800** buys today.
Safe, yes, but every year they buy a bit less
Well spotted! He's not losing euros: he's losing **purchasing power**. Whatever he won't need for years can be put to work to beat inflation.
Better take it out and keep it at home
In a drawer it loses out to inflation just the same… and it can get lost or stolen too.
Huh… I'd never thought of it like that.
Careful: the Deposit Guarantee Fund protects up to **€100,000** if the bank goes bust.
It protects your euros, not your purchasing power.
Try it: in the simulator, put €1,000 of virtual money to work in a global ETF.
An incredible offer
Nico
I've found a fund that **doubles your money in 2 years** with no risk.
Are you in? Places are only open today.
What do you think?
I'm in! Sounds great
Doubling in 2 years takes **36 % a year**. Nobody offers that risk-free.
Doubling in 2 years with no risk is impossible: it smells like a scam
Well spotted! And the rush («today only») is another classic scam sign.
I'll ask him to explain it and put in half
Not even half: check it on the CNMV website first.
There's a trick to catch these promises in seconds: the **rule of 72**.
When does it double?
**72 ÷ return** = the years it takes your investment to double. Move the return and check it.
At 6 % a year, how many years does it take for €1,000 to double?
In 6 years
In about 12 years
In about 20 years
72 ÷ 6 = **12 years**. The exact maths gives 11.9: the rule of 72 is almost spot on.
Find the return that doubles your money in about 8 years.
**72 ÷ return = years to double**: it tells you how much a fee, a debt or an impossible promise weighs. Try it: in Market, open the S&P 500 with monthly candles and find when it doubled.
This works for debt too: a card at 24 % doubles what you owe in 3 years.
At 2 %, 36 years to double! That's about what inflation usually runs at…
Move the return and watch the stack of notes grow

u1l1-1.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
u1l1-1.explanation: Income and savings are flows (every month); net worth is a snapshot at one moment.
right: What you don't spend of what comes in
What you own minus what you owe
Putting savings to work to produce more

u1l1-4.prompt: Someone who earns €4,000 a month and spends it all can have a lower net worth than someone who earns €1,500 and saves €300.
u1l1-4.explanation: Net worth grows with what you save and invest, not with what you earn.

u1l1-5.prompt: Is it income or net worth?
options: The rent you collect every month
u1l1-5.explanation: Income is what comes in; net worth is what you build up.

u1l1-7.prompt: Net worth = what you own − what you ____.
u1l1-7.explanation: Debts subtract: a €15,000 car with a €12,000 loan only adds €3,000 to you.

u1l1-10.prompt: You get a €200 a month pay rise. You already have an emergency fund and no expensive debt. What will grow your net worth most over the next 10 years?
options: Changing your car, now that you can afford a bigger instalment
Investing part of it every month, automatically
Leaving it in your current account and deciding later
u1l1-10.explanation: Net worth grows by putting the difference aside and investing it. A new car is tempting, but it turns the rise into debt on something that loses value.
feedback: The rise goes on instalments and on a car that loses value every year: your net worth barely moves.
You put it aside before you see it and invest it: compound interest works for you for 10 years.
With no plan, the money ends up spent, and whatever's left loses purchasing power.

u1l1-11.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Net worth is what you earn each month, so it doesn't change
It depends on what you still owe and what it's worth now
u1l1-11.explanation: The car adds at what it's worth today, not what it cost, and the loan subtracts. It's tempting to count the purchase price, but the debt and the wear eat into it.
feedback: That's your income: net worth is what you build up.
That's it! Net worth is what you own minus what you owe, at today's prices.
You still have to subtract what you owe on the loan, and the car is worth less every year.
lines: I've bought a €25,000 car on finance.
So now I have €25,000 of net worth, right?

u1l2-2.explanation: It's 2 % in the medium term. That's why idle money loses value even in normal years.

u1l2-4.prompt: What can push prices up? Tick all that apply.
options: The central bank raising rates sharply
A lot of money being created very quickly
People saving more and spending less
u1l2-4.explanation: Creating a lot of money quickly or dearer energy pushes prices up, just as demand outstripping supply does. Raising rates or spending less holds them back.

u1l2-5.prompt: Match each situation with its effect on prices.
options: Everyone wants to buy at once
u1l2-5.explanation: Cost-push inflation, demand-pull inflation and the ECB's tool for curbing both.

u1l2-6.prompt: It's 2022: inflation in Spain hits 8 % and your account pays 0 %. You have €10,000 you won't need for 10 years. What do you do?
options: Look for options that can beat inflation
Nothing: in the bank it's safe and can't lose value
Spend it all before it's worth less
u1l2-6.explanation: Idle money isn't safe from inflation. Money you won't need for years should be put to work.
feedback: Good: over 10 years, leaving it idle is the surest way to lose purchasing power.
Your €10,000 buys 8 % less in a year: about €800 of purchasing power gone.
Spending out of fear doesn't protect your future: it just swaps saving for consumption.

u1l2-8.prompt: Over 20 years, does this usually protect your money from inflation?
options: An ETF of shares from all over the world
A deposit at 1 % with inflation at 3 %
u1l2-8.explanation: When everything goes up, companies raise their prices too: that's why, over the long run, diversified shares have usually beaten inflation, with bad years along the way. Idle money, or money earning less than prices rise, loses purchasing power even if the balance doesn't go down.

u1l2-9.prompt: The news breaks: inflation is rising more than expected and there's talk of the ECB raising rates. Your global ETF dips a little that day. You're investing for 20 years from now. What do you do?
options: Sell everything and get back in when inflation comes down
Carry on with my contributions as usual
Move it all to my current account
u1l2-9.explanation: With high inflation, idle money loses more than ever. Selling over a headline is tempting, but it swaps your 20-year plan for a one-day scare.
feedback: Nobody knows when it will pass, and out of the market your money loses against prices again.
A headline moves the price for a few days; over 20 years, what counts is to keep investing.
Precisely when inflation is high, idle money is what loses most.

options: What an average Spanish household earns a year
u1l3-1.explanation: It's a consumer price index: it compares the same basket over time.

u1l3-3.prompt: Your personal inflation can differ from the official figure.
u1l3-3.explanation: The CPI weights items by average spending; your basket gives each thing a different weight.

u1l3-5.prompt: If electricity shoots up one month, headline CPI jumps a lot, but ____ inflation barely moves.
u1l3-5.explanation: Core inflation excludes energy to show the underlying trend.

u1l3-7.prompt: Match each profile with the part of the basket that affects them most.
u1l3-7.explanation: Every household has its own basket: that's why personal inflation varies.

u1l3-9.prompt: What's true about the CPI? Tick all.
options: It compares prices with the same month the year before
It measures how much wages rise
Each product is weighted by average household spending
The Banco de España publishes it once a year
u1l3-9.explanation: The CPI compares prices with the same month the year before and weights each product by average household spending. The INE publishes it every month, and it doesn't measure wages.

u1l3-10.prompt: You rent in an expensive city and your personal inflation is 5 %, even though official CPI is 3 %. You're investing for 20 years from now. What does this tell you?
options: Nothing: only the official CPI counts
That I have to beat my own inflation
That investing isn't worth it if prices rise that much
u1l3-10.explanation: Your personal inflation is the bar your money has to clear. It's tempting to look only at the official figure, but your basket can rise more than the average.
feedback: CPI is the average; what you pay depends on your own basket.
Exactly: your bar is your own inflation, not the average. Money that earns little loses against your prices.
Quite the opposite: with prices rising, idle money is what loses most.

u1l4-2.prompt: If your account pays 3 % and inflation is 2 %, you gain purchasing power.

u1l4-3.prompt: Inflation at 2.5 %. Do you gain or lose purchasing power?
u1l4-3.explanation: You only gain if you earn more than inflation.

u1l4-4.prompt: What does the Fondo de Garantía de Depósitos (Spain's deposit guarantee scheme) protect?
options: Up to €100,000 per person per bank
u1l4-4.explanation: It protects the euros you've deposited if the bank goes bust, not against inflation or stock market falls.

u1l4-6.explanation: It's the quick way to tell whether your money is gaining or losing purchasing power.

u1l4-10.prompt: You have €6,000: €3,000 is your emergency fund and you won't touch the other €3,000 for 15 years. How do you organise it?
options: All in the 0 % account: that way it's safe and always within reach
The cushion within reach; the rest invested long term
All in the ETF, emergency fund included
u1l4-10.explanation: Each euro according to its time frame: what you might need tomorrow, available and risk-free; what you won't touch for years, invested. Putting it all in the ETF is tempting, but it leaves you with no emergency fund.
feedback: The long-term €3,000 loses purchasing power for 15 years.
The emergency fund stays to hand and the long-term money works to beat inflation.
If something unexpected comes up in the middle of a fall, you'll have to sell at a loss.

u1l4-11.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Better take it out and spend it before it's worth less
You gain euros, but you lose purchasing power
u1l4-11.explanation: If your money earns less than inflation, your real return is negative even if the balance goes up. It's tempting to look only at the 2 %, but what matters is what you can buy with it.
feedback: Spending out of fear doesn't protect your future: it just swaps saving for spending.
You gain euros, but prices rise faster than your balance.
That's it! It earns less than inflation: money you won't need soon can aim higher.
lines: My bank pays me 2 % and inflation is at 2.7 %.
At least I'm earning something, right?

u1l6-4.prompt: Match each return with the years it takes to double.

u1l6-7.prompt: The rule of 72 also works for inflation: at 3 %, prices double in about 24 years.

u1l6-8.prompt: To double your money in under 10 years, what return do you need?
u1l6-8.explanation: Under 10 years requires more than 7.2 % a year (72 ÷ 10).

u1l6-10.prompt: Two funds track the same global index. One charges 0.2 % a year and the other 2 %. You'll invest for 30 years. Which do you choose?
options: It doesn't matter: the difference is tiny
The 2 % one: if it charges more, it must be better
u1l6-10.explanation: With the same index, the fee is the only thing that changes, and it comes off your return every year: with a lower return, your money takes longer to double. Thinking expensive means better is tempting, but here you're not buying anything extra.
feedback: 2 % a year delays each doubling by several years, and over 30 years that weighs a huge amount.
They track the same index: the only thing that changes is what they take from you each year.
You keep almost all the return: your money doubles quite a bit sooner.

u1l6-11.prompt: Mark the promises the rule of 72 exposes as impossible.
options: 12-month deposit at 2 % APR, covered by the Deposit Guarantee Fund.
Global index fund. Past returns don't guarantee future returns.
3 % a month guaranteed. Places limited until tonight.
Double your money in 6 months, guaranteed and risk-free.
u1l6-11.explanation: Doubling in 6 months or earning a «guaranteed» 3 % a month are huge returns nobody can guarantee: the rule of 72 gives them away in seconds. Legitimate offers explain the risk and don't rush you.

u1l6-12.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Invest: the stock market goes up in the long run
u1l6-12.explanation: The rule of 72 also works for what you owe: at 24 %, the debt doubles in about 3 years. Investing is tempting, but no investment guarantees you'll earn at that pace.
feedback: That's it! Getting rid of 24 % is earning a guaranteed 24 %.
At 24 %, your debt doubles in about 3 years: no investment guarantees you that.
Better than nothing, but you leave alive a debt that grows very fast.

Should I invest or pay off the card?
